catalog_quote: In Lemi Chin, full syllables bear tone, whereas minor syllables are phonologically toneless, surfacing with a neutral mid pitch. Minor syllables in Lemi Chin also reflect other constraints that are widespread in Southeast Asian languages. The duration is noticeably short in comparison to full syllables, producing an iambic rhythm. Onset consonants in these syllables are restricted in number and complexity of phonemic features. Phonetic vowel quality is loosely restricted to a range of mid-central vowel qualities. These same features are evident in several of the Kanise Khumi prefixes, notably the valency-increasing prefixes p- and t-, and the adjectivizer k-. With predictable mid pitch, these prefixes support an analysis based on syllable structure in which full syllables are tone-bearing and minor syllables are toneless. ... The strong preference for iambic rhythm in Kanise Khumi words means that non-final syllables almost always get “reduced” in lexical derivation. Lower amplitude, intensity, and shorter duration is usually evident even with compounds in Kanise Khumi.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Eastern Khumi (Kanise Khumi; likewise Lemi per Herr 2011) is a tone language (three lexical tones on major syllables). Words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables or disyllables with an iambic (weak-strong) rhythm: prosodic prominence sits on the word-final major syllable, while non-final minor syllables/prefixes are unstressed, toneless (default mid pitch), reduced in vowel quality and about a quarter of the duration; even compound first members show reduced amplitude and duration. Tan 2022a states the same explicitly ('iambic languages like Kanise'; prominence word-final, 'computed over tonal contrast').
new_statements.exceptions: Tan 2022a (pp.36-42): productive prefixes a(ŋ)-, ka(ŋ)- and first members of productive compounds are full, tone-bearing syllables with near-equal prominence (only phonetically weakened at the left edge); some non-compound disyllables are 'trochaic', their first syllable /'CV(N)-/ having equal or greater prominence than the final syllable, and are not analysed as sesquisyllables. Ikeda 2022: prefix ʔɜ- carries high (Tone 1) pitch and is separable, unlike toneless p-, t-, k-, s-.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word in citation forms (verbs and nouns from Bryant's 2020 recorded wordlist, one main educated male speaker, slow careful speech); prominence is described as word-final rhythm/tonal contrast rather than a separate contrastive stress; Herr 2011 for Lemi gives tone and minor-syllable facts but deliberately no stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Two cek varieties are described: Herr 2011 covers Lemi (autonym Lemi, exonym Akelong; formerly called 'Mro'; Paletwa Township), Tan 2022a/b, Ikeda 2022 and Ikeda et al. 2026 cover Kanise Khumi (name adopted 2016 for the Nideun/Tahaensae/Uiphaw clans near Sami town, Paletwa Township; ~5,800 people), which 'is associated with the ISO 639-3 code [cek] Eastern Khumi, but this label reflects linguistic similarity rather than a shared ethnolinguistic identity' (Ikeda et al. 2026: 2). Glottolog east2779 lists no dialect sub-codes. The quoted stress/rhythm statement is for Kanise Khumi, with the Lemi facts (Herr 2011) matching. Grierson's LSI 'Khami' and Peterson's Khumi are Bangladesh Khumi (khum1248), not this language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-tone language (Ikeda 2022: Tone 1 high level modal, Tone 2 short mid glottalized, Tone 3 falling low breathy, on full syllables). Words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic with iambic rhythm: the non-final minor syllable (prefixes p-, t-, k-, s-, and mostly the agreement marker ʔɜ-) is short, of low amplitude/intensity, toneless with a default mid pitch, and unstressed / prosodically non-prominent; the final full (major) syllable is the prominent, tone-bearing one. No independent contrastive word stress is described; prominence is stated as a rhythm/reduction pattern, not a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Ikeda 2022 pp.158-159: the full-syllable prefixes a(ŋ)- and ka(ŋ)- and the agreement marker ʔɜ- still sit in the iambic (weak, non-final) position but keep a coda and a specified tone (a(ŋ)- Tone 1, ka(ŋ)- Tone 2, ʔɜ- high), so 'it does not seem likely that all affixes in Kanise Khumi are toneless'; reduction of non-final syllables holds 'even with compounds'. Tan 2022b p.343 frames the 'lack of stress' on minor syllables as a possibility that explains vowel undershoot, not as a demonstrated stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: All three JSEALS papers and Ikeda 2021 describe the Kanise Khumi variety (Sami town area, Paletwa Township, Chin State, Myanmar; ISO code [cek] Eastern Khumi; Bryant 2020 word list, main speaker Ezra), while the 'In Lemi Chin, full syllables bear tone..' sentence in Ikeda 2022 p.158 summarises Herr 2011 on Lemi Chin (spoken just north of Kanise, 74% lexical similarity) before extending the same pattern to Kanise prefixes p-, t-, k-. The catalog item 'Kanise Khumi, with Lemi Chin' covers both varieties under east2779.

tone_statements.citation: Baleno, Grace. 2024. Tone in Kanise Khumi nouns. M.A. thesis, Trinity Western University (CanIL).
tone_statements.quote: Kanise Khumi has three pitch heights, H, M, and L, and three phonemic tones, /H/, /M/, and /L/. There is also evidence for an optional phrase-final low boundary tone. Tone behaves differently between full major syllables and reduced minor syllables. Minor syllables are unstressed, initial syllables in sesquisyllabic forms … The three-way contrast (H vs M vs L) is found only on minor syllables of historically complex sesquisyllabic nouns. Simultaneously, major syllables have non-contrastive H, M, and L pitch heights alongside contrastive vowel phonation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 35, Chapter 4 'Tone in Kanise Khumi nouns', opening paragraph; restated p. 64 (4.5) and p. 65 (5.1)
tone_statements.summary: Nouns: three level tones H, M, L, contrastive only on unstressed minor (prefix) syllables; major syllables contrast phonation (modal/creaky/breathy) with predictable pitch; optional final L boundary.
